text: Mary Letitia Caldwell (December 18, 1890 – July 1, 1972) was an American chemist who taught chemistry at Western College, where she earned her bachelor's degree in 1913 and taught until 1918. Born in Bogotá, Colombia, to U.S. missionaries, she was part of a family of five siblings who all valued higher education. She earned her M.A. and Ph.D. from Columbia University in 1919 and 1921, respectively, and was hired as an instructor at Columbia in 1922. She became the first woman instructor in the chemistry department at Columbia University and later the first woman to attain the rank of assistant professor there in 1948, eventually becoming a full professor in 1948. She was the only female member of the senior faculty in the chemistry department at Columbia University. Caldwell had a progressive muscular disorder that made her reliant on a wheelchair for life, beginning to use it by 1960, and her 9th floor office at Chandler Hall remained unchanged despite this. She spent sixty years researching amylase, a starch enzyme, and developed a method for purifying crystalline porcine pancreatic amylase, which is now used by laboratories in America and Europe. In 1960, she received the Garvan Medal from the American Chemical Society, an annual honor awarded to a U.S. female chemist for significant contributions to chemistry. Her work focused on purifying enzymes, as she was dissatisfied with commercial enzyme materials, and she successfully developed a method for isolating crystalline pancreatic enzymes.
